title: Vomiting in a patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor — recognising and responding to a time-critical presentation

blocks.text: Vomiting in a patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor — recognising and responding to a time-critical presentation
AMaC MRCP PACES23 · R5-202 · Station 2, acute consultation · Skills A–G (focus C, E, F, G) · 20 minutes · Prepared 14 October 2026 · Educational simulation; not an official PACES mark scheme.

A 47-year-old with diabetes taking empagliflozin reports vomiting, abdominal pain and rapid breathing. Capillary glucose is 9.8 mmol/L. Speak to the patient (and accompanying person if applicable), identify immediate risks and explain your management plan. The examiner may provide results on request.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: HOOK — Possible SGLT2 inhibitor-associated euglycaemic DKA: normal or mildly elevated glucose does not exclude significant ketosis and acidosis.

TRAP — Do not falsely reassure because capillary glucose is below conventional hyperglycaemic DKA values. Treat ketonaemia and acidosis, investigate precipitant and give SGLT2 sick-day guidance after recovery.

rows: “I need to check how unwell you are first.”
ABCDE, observations, immediate escalation as needed.
“Your symptoms can signal a serious medical complication.”
SGLT2 inhibitor, insulin omission/reduction, illness or reduced intake, pregnancy or surgery; assess dehydration, respiratory rate, Kussmaul breathing, consciousness and haemodynamics.
“We will act while tests are underway.”

Immediately check capillary blood ketones, venous pH/bicarbonate, electrolytes including potassium, renal function and glucose; stop SGLT2 inhibitor. If DKA is confirmed, initiate local JBDS fixed-rate IV insulin and fluid protocol with early dextrose where indicated, monitoring potassium closely and seeking diabetes-team support.
“I will tell you what we are monitoring closely.”

blocks.text: Patient: “My sugar is under ten, so how can this be dangerous?” If asked, you take empagliflozin and have recently had poor intake with vomiting. You feel frightened by rapid breathing. If dismissed, say, “I am getting more breathless.” Do not volunteer venous gas or ketones unless the candidate requests appropriate testing.

History and examination information available when requested: SGLT2 inhibitor, insulin omission/reduction, illness or reduced intake, pregnancy or surgery; assess dehydration, respiratory rate, Kussmaul breathing, consciousness and haemodynamics.

Q1 EXAMINER: “How can this be DKA when glucose is 9.8 mmol/L?” MODEL: SGLT2 inhibitors may cause euglycaemic DKA. Confirm with capillary blood ketones and venous gas; glucose alone cannot rule it out.

Q2 EXAMINER: “Which investigations must be obtained now?” MODEL: ABCDE observations, blood ketones, venous pH/bicarbonate, electrolytes especially potassium, renal function and glucose, with an assessment of the precipitant.
Q3 EXAMINER: “What should happen to empagliflozin?” MODEL: Stop it during the acute illness and arrange senior diabetes review before any future use.

Q4 EXAMINER: “What is the key treatment principle?” MODEL: Urgent monitored DKA treatment with fluids, insulin to clear ketones and additional glucose when needed to prevent hypoglycaemia; monitor potassium.
Q5 EXAMINER: “What if the patient deteriorates?” MODEL: Call the acute/critical-care team, repeat ABCDE and continue resuscitation and physiological monitoring.
Curveball: Patient becomes hypotensive or less responsive. Candidate must stop routine questioning, call for help, reassess ABCDE, monitor and treat reversible causes.
• [R1] Pass: Introduces self, initiates ABCDE, observations and urgent clinical support. High-performance: Explains parallel resuscitation and communication, with continuous reassessment.

• [R2] Pass: Elicits SGLT2 inhibitor, recent food/fluid intake, vomiting, illness and insulin changes. High-performance: Asks about surgery, infection and ketogenic diet and correlates onset with exposure.

• [R3] Pass: Recognises DKA despite non-high glucose; requests blood ketones and venous pH/bicarbonate immediately. High-performance: Interprets ketones, acid-base results and anion gap in the clinical context.

• [R4] Pass: Explains likely euglycaemic DKA and evaluates infection, pancreatitis and other causes of acidosis. High-performance: Avoids premature closure while prioritising life-threatening ketosis/acidosis.

• [R5] Pass: Withholds SGLT2 inhibitor; escalates to urgent DKA pathway with IV fluids, insulin and glucose as indicated, checking potassium. High-performance: Explains why insulin to stop ketogenesis can require concurrent dextrose and electrolyte monitoring.
• [R6] Pass: Explains why vomiting and rapid breathing need hospital treatment despite glucose reading. High-performance: Uses teach-back and communicates carefully without blaming missed treatment.

• [R7] Pass: Arranges close observations, glucose/ketone/electrolyte monitoring and acute medical assessment. High-performance: Plans trigger management and sick-day safety advice only after stabilisation.
FAIL — CANDIDATE: “Your glucose is 9.8, so this is not DKA. You can go home.” PATIENT: “But I keep vomiting and breathing quickly.” CANDIDATE: “No tests are needed.” [Unsafe: misses euglycaemic DKA.]

PASS — CANDIDATE: “You may have a dangerous build-up of acids even when your glucose is not high. I am asking for urgent help and checking blood ketones and acidity while we assess and treat you.” PATIENT: “Could the tablet be involved?” CANDIDATE: “Yes, we will stop it now, treat the emergency and check your salts and hydration.”

HIGH-PERFORMANCE — CANDIDATE: “I am assessing your breathing and circulation immediately, placing you on monitoring and calling the acute team. We must check ketones, venous gas and potassium. If DKA is confirmed we will start the monitored DKA pathway; glucose may be needed alongside insulin even with a reading under ten. I will also investigate what triggered this and explain the recovery plan once safe.”
R2/R4: Overlooks discriminating presentation: Possible SGLT2 inhibitor-associated euglycaemic DKA: normal or mildly elevated glucose does not exclude significant ketosis and acidosis.

R5: Defers urgent treatment until every result returns: Immediately check capillary blood ketones, venous pH/bicarbonate, electrolytes including potassium, renal function and glucose; stop SGLT2 inhibitor. If DKA is confirmed, initiate local JBDS fixed-rate IV insulin and fluid protocol with early dextrose where indicated, monitoring potassium closely and seeking diabetes-team support.

R7: Fails to identify specific danger: Do not falsely reassure because capillary glucose is below conventional hyperglycaemic DKA values. Treat ketonaemia and acidosis, investigate precipitant and give SGLT2 sick-day guidance after recovery.
“This glucose reading does not rule out DKA; I need ketones and a venous gas now.”
“I will stop the SGLT2 inhibitor and urgently involve the DKA team.”
“I will check potassium and glucose while treating ketosis, using additional glucose with insulin if required.”

THINK: SGLT2 euglycaemic DKA. SAY: recognise urgency. DO: immediately assess, monitor, investigate and treat according to UK protocol. TRAP: Normal glucose does not exclude DKA.
